title: Picarones
subtitle: Peruvian pumpkin and sweet potato doughnuts with chancaca syrup
excerpt: Picarones are ring-shaped Peruvian doughnuts made from a yeast dough of mashed pumpkin and sweet potato. They are fried until golden and served hot with a dark aromatic syrup made from chancaca, cinnamon and star anise. They are one of the most popular street desserts in Lima.
sourceNotes: Picarones were created in Lima during the colonial period as a local adaptation of Spanish buneulos. Cooks substituted pumpkin and sweet potato, both native Andean ingredients, for the original dough base. The chancaca syrup is a defining feature of the dish and gives it its distinctive caramel depth.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The chancaca syrup can be made up to 3 days ahead and kept in the fridge. Reheat gently before serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: Unrefined cane sugar used in Peru and other South American countries, similar to piloncillo in Mexico. It is melted into a dark aromatic syrup poured over picarones.

content.text: This recipe makes 16 picarones and takes about 50 minutes of active work plus 1 hour of resting time for the dough to prove. You combine mashed pumpkin and sweet potato with flour and yeast to make a soft, slightly sticky dough. The rings are shaped by hand and dropped into hot oil, then drizzled with

The dough is wetter than most doughnut doughs. Wetting your hands before shaping each ring makes it much easier to handle. Make the syrup before you start frying so it is warm and ready when the picarones come out of the oil. The syrup should be pourable but thick enough to coat the back of a spoon.

items.prepNote: or dark brown sugar for the syrup

content.text: Boil 250g diced pumpkin or butternut squash and 250g diced sweet potato separately until very tender. Drain well and mash together until smooth. Leave to cool to warm, not hot.
Dissolve 7g fast-action yeast in 3 tbsp warm water with 1 tbsp sugar. Leave for 5 minutes until frothy.

Combine the mashed vegetables, yeast mixture and 200g plain flour in a bowl. Mix until a soft, slightly sticky dough forms. It will be looser than bread dough. Cover with a clean cloth and leave in a warm place for 1 hour until puffed.

Make the syrup while the dough rests. Combine 100g piloncillo or dark brown sugar, the cinnamon stick, 1 star anise, a strip of orange peel and 200ml water in a small saucepan. Simmer for 10 to 15 minutes until reduced to a thick, pourable syrup. Strain and keep warm.
Heat 5 to 6cm of vegetable oil in a deep saucepan to 175C. Use a thermometer to check the temperature.
Wet your hands. Take a golf-ball-sized piece of dough, poke a hole through the centre with your thumb, and stretch it gently into a ring about 8cm across. Drop carefully into the oil.
Fry in batches of 3 to 4, turning once, for 3 to 4 minutes per side until golden brown all over. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on kitchen paper.
Serve immediately, drizzled generously with the warm chancaca syrup.

attrs.symptom: Dough is too sticky to shape
attrs.cause: The mashed vegetables had too much moisture
attrs.fix: Drain the cooked vegetables very thoroughly and let them cool before mashing. Wet your hands rather than adding more flour, which makes the picarones dense.

attrs.cause: The oil was not hot enough when the dough went in
attrs.fix: Check the oil temperature with a thermometer and bring it back to 175C between batches. Too cool and the dough absorbs oil rather than sealing.

attrs.cause: It was not reduced for long enough
attrs.fix: Continue simmering until the syrup coats the back of a spoon. It should fall in a slow drizzle, not a fast pour.

content.text: Picarones are one of Lima's most beloved street foods, sold from large vats of oil by vendors who shape and fry them to order. They are also served at family celebrations and appear on the dessert menus of traditional Peruvian restaurants.
